result.summary: Ulysses reveals his name to the Phaeacians and begins telling of his wanderings. He recounts the raid on the Cicons, the Lotus-eaters, and his capture in the cave of the Cyclops Polyphemus, whom he blinds and escapes. Polyphemus prays to Neptune to doom Ulysses' homecoming.

scenes.title: Ulysses names himself
scenes.summary: Ulysses praises the feast and the bard, then reveals his name and home, and says he will tell his adventures.

scenes.title: The Cicons and the storm
scenes.summary: Ulysses sacks Ismarus, but his disobedient men are routed by the Cicons. A storm sent by Jove then drives the fleet off course near Cape Malea.
scenes.stakes: Ulysses' men risk death through their greed and disobedience, and then through the storm.

scenes.title: Land of the Lotus-eaters
scenes.summary: Men sent ashore eat the lotus and forget home. Ulysses drags them back to the ships and sails on.
scenes.stakes: His men could lose all desire to return home.

scenes.title: The goat island
scenes.summary: After describing the Cyclopes and the island, Ulysses lands in darkness and hunts goats. He then decides to scout the Cyclopes' land.

place.name: Island off the land of the Cyclopes

scenes.title: Trapped in the Cyclops' cave
scenes.summary: Ulysses and twelve men enter the cave. Polyphemus returns, seals it with a stone, and eats two men. Ulysses lies about his ship.
scenes.stakes: Ulysses and his men are trapped and will be eaten one by one.

scenes.title: Wine, Noman, and blinding
scenes.summary: Ulysses prepares a stake, gets Polyphemus drunk with Maron's wine, calls himself Noman, and blinds him. The other Cyclopes leave, thinking no man harms him.
scenes.stakes: Failure would mean the death of Ulysses and every companion.

scenes.title: Escape under the rams
scenes.summary: Ulysses ties his men beneath rams and clings under the best ram himself. They escape past the blinded Cyclops to the ship.
scenes.stakes: Discovery by the blind Cyclops would mean death.

scenes.title: Taunts and Polyphemus' curse
scenes.summary: Ulysses taunts Polyphemus and reveals his name. The Cyclops hurls rocks and prays to Neptune. Ulysses rejoins his fleet and sails on.
scenes.stakes: Neptune's wrath threatens Ulysses' homecoming and the lives of his remaining men.

alias_notes.explanation: A false name Ulysses gives Polyphemus, making the Cyclopes think no man attacks him.
Polyphemus is called simply the Cyclops until the other Cyclopes name him.

notable_quotes.reason: Ulysses' Noman trick, the cleverest ruse of the poem.
Ulysses' proud boast reveals his name and brings Neptune's curse.
Expresses the poem's central love of home and country.

analysis.text: Cunning (metis) defeats brute strength, but Ulysses' pride in revealing his name shows how his flaws bring suffering.
Hospitality (xenia) is central: the Cyclopes ignore it and Polyphemus violates it, in contrast to the Phaeacians and Maron.

legacy.text: The Noman trick and the blinding of Polyphemus inspired Euripides' satyr play Cyclops and countless later retellings.
The Coen brothers' film O Brother, Where Art Thou? (2000) includes a one-eyed Cyclops figure drawing on this episode.

fun_facts.text: The story of a man blinding a giant by trickery has folk-tale parallels across Europe and Asia.

language_notes.text: "May become my guests" refers to the Phaeacians one day visiting Ulysses in Ithaca, returning the hospitality he is receiving now.
"Squat" means low-lying; "It" is Ithaca, which Ulysses describes as lying low and farthest west, toward the sunset.
"Aeaean" means of Aeaea, the island where Circe lived.
"The time when men loose their oxen" means late afternoon, when farm work ends and the oxen are unyoked.
"Thrice invoked" refers to the custom of calling each dead man's name three times to honour the dead and call his spirit home.
"Doubling" a cape means sailing around it.
"Thence" means from there, i.e. from the place where the storm had driven him after the Cicons; "for a space" means for a period.
"Made them fast under the benches" means tied them up beneath the rowers' seats in the ships so they could not escape.
"Munching lotus": the lotus here is a legendary honey-sweet plant that causes forgetfulness, not the water lily of today.
"Smote the grey sea with their oars" is a formulaic way of saying they rowed.
"Trust in providence" means they rely on the gods to make food grow without their labour.
"Fed down" means grazed by livestock; the island is neither farmed nor used for pasture.
"Colonised" refers to Greek settlement of new lands overseas, a practice familiar to the poem's audience.
"Jove's daughters" are nymphs of the wild, said here to drive the goats toward the hunters. Jove is the Greek Zeus.
"Exploit" here means explore or investigate, not take advantage of.
"Laurels" are bay trees, evergreen shrubs with glossy leaves, common in Mediterranean lands.
A talent was a large unit of weight, used for measuring gold and silver; seven talents is a very rich gift.
"Hoggets" are young sheep in their second year. "Whey" is the watery liquid left when milk curdles into cheese.
"Hands against every man" means living as pirates, attacking everyone and being attacked in return.
"Suppliants" are people who humbly beg for protection or help, which the gods were thought to guard.
Neptune (the Greek Poseidon) is the sea god; blaming him is a plausible lie, and he is also the Cyclops' father.
"Vouchsafed" means condescended to give; here it stresses the Cyclops' contemptuous silence.
"Shoo, shoo" renders the Cyclops's herding cry; the translator gives it a homely, modern sound.
"Fine it evenly off" means to smooth and taper the log's end so it can be sharpened to a point.
"Ramping and raving" means rampaging and behaving wildly; "further me on my way" means help me travel homeward.
Nectar and Ambrosia were the drink and food of the gods, so the Cyclops is praising the wine as divine.
"Noman" is the name Ulysses gives himself; in Greek it puns on "no one" (outis), which makes the later trick work.
An auger is a hand tool for boring holes, here turned by a strap wound round the drill and pulled by two men.
Neptune (the Greek Poseidon) is Polyphemus's father, so the Cyclopes tell him to appeal to his own divine parent.
Withies are flexible willow twigs, used here as cords to bind the sheep together.
"Esconced" means settled snugly and securely, here hidden in the wool.
"Child of morning, rosy-fingered Dawn" is a fixed Homeric formula for daybreak, personifying Dawn as a goddess.
"Not wont" means not accustomed; "mead" here means meadow.
Noman is the false name Ulysses gave earlier; the Cyclops takes it literally, which is why he cannot name his attacker.
"Smote" is an archaic past tense of smite, meaning struck; the rowers beat the water with their oars.
"Your sin would find you out" means your wrong would eventually bring punishment; Ulysses presents the Cyclops' breach of hospitality as an offence against the gods.
The rudder here is the steering oar at the stern; the rock lands just behind the ship.
"Spoiled your beauty" is mocking understatement for blinding Polyphemus.
The "old prophecy" refers to Telemus' prediction, explained in the next sentence.
Hades is the god of the dead, and also the name of his underworld realm, the "house of Hades".
The bracketed lines are marked by the translator as a doubtful or later addition; the 'another man's ship' detail matches Ulysses' eventual return.
Burning the thigh bones was the standard Greek sacrificial offering to the gods.
Hawsers are the thick ropes that moor a ship.

context_notes.text: Ulysses is replying to Alcinous, king of the Phaeacians, after the bard Demodocus has sung of the Trojan War and moved him to tears.
Calypso and Circe are goddesses who each detained Ulysses for a long time, Calypso on her island and Circe on Aeaea.
The Cicons were a Thracian people allied with Troy, so Ulysses raids them on his way home.
Cape Malea is the southern tip of the Peloponnese, a dangerous point for sailors. Cythera lies just beyond it.
The Cyclopes are one-eyed giants. Ulysses has not yet said so here, but the following episode with Polyphemus will show their savagery.
Dawn's stock description, "rosy-fingered," appears repeatedly in Homer's poems to mark the start of a new day.
Ulysses' twelve ships are the fleet he brought from Troy. The Cicons were raided just before, in Book 9, which is where the wine came from.
Ismarus was a city of the Cicones in Thrace, which Ulysses and his men had just sacked. Apollo was god of prophecy, music and healing.
Offering part of the food to the gods before eating was standard custom, and shows the men acting as proper, pious guests.
The Cyclopes were a race of giant one-eyed shepherds, here shown as lawless and scornful of the gods.
Ulysses uses the strong wine given to him earlier by Maron, a priest of Apollo, to overcome the Cyclops.
Blacksmiths hardened hot iron by quenching it in cold water, a familiar craft image for the original audience.
The Cyclopes live scattered in separate caves without community or law, so neighbours come only when they hear his cries.
Polyphemus is the Cyclops, a one-eyed giant and son of Neptune, whom Ulysses has just blinded with a heated stake.
Taking the Cyclops' fat sheep as plunder fits the heroic custom of seizing spoils, and repays the men eaten in the cave.
Seers like Telemus were believed to foresee the future through divine insight; their prophecies in Greek stories usually come true.
Neptune (the Greek Poseidon) is god of the sea. Polyphemus is his son, which makes the curse that follows dangerous for Ulysses.

literary_notes.text: Ulysses boasts of his fame for subtlety, presenting himself as the clever hero before telling a tale in which his cleverness is tested.
Ulysses says no splendid foreign home can match one's own country and parents, stating the central theme of homecoming.
The arriving Cicons are compared to leaves and flowers in summer, conveying their overwhelming numbers.
Night is said to spring forth out of the heavens, making the sudden darkness of the storm seem like a living force.
The lotus offers forgetfulness and comfort in exchange for homecoming, a temptation to abandon the central goal of the journey.
The Cyclopes are defined by what they lack: ships, craft and community, which shows their separation from civilization.
"Rosy-fingered Dawn" is a fixed Homeric epithet, giving a formal rhythm to the narrative and marking the passage of time.
Ulysses' curiosity about whether the Cyclopes are savage or hospitable foreshadows the dangerous encounter in the cave.
Comparing the Cyclops to a crag on a mountaintop conveys his huge, inhuman, rock-like size.
Ulysses' admission that leaving would have been better hints at the disaster his curiosity and desire for gifts will cause.
Ulysses' quick, deceptive answer displays his cunning, the trait that defines him throughout the poem.
Likening the men to puppies shows how little the Cyclops values them and makes the violence more shocking.
The lion comparison presents the Cyclops as a ravenous beast, stressing his lack of civilization.
Comparing the huge stone to a quiver lid shows Polyphemus's enormous strength by making the boulder seem trivial.
The Cyclops promises the guest-gift of eating Noman last, a grim perversion of hospitality that he thinks generous.
The auger comparison turns a horrific act into a familiar shipwright's task, showing the men's steady, practised teamwork.
Polyphemus's truthful-sounding cry means "no man is hurting me" to the others, so Ulysses' false name deceives them.
The great hero escapes by clinging helplessly under a sheep, a humble position that reverses his earlier boasts of strength.
Ulysses calls himself "my crafty self", stressing the cunning that defines him throughout the poem.
The Cyclops speaks tenderly to the ram while the reader knows the enemy he seeks is hanging beneath it.
Polyphemus addresses the ram as if it could answer, which shows his pathos and his violent rage.
Ulysses' rage and pride override his men's caution, showing the recklessness that brings the curse on him.
Polyphemus expected a mighty hero, yet his own prophecy was fulfilled by a cunning man he calls weak.
The curse outlines Ulysses' long delayed return, the loss of all his men and the trouble awaiting him at home.
Jove's refusal of the sacrifice hints that the gods' favour is turning against Ulysses' fleet.
"Rosy-fingered Dawn" is a recurring Homeric epithet that marks the passage of time.
